title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Key Concepts
‘dplyr’ Functions

filter() // pick rows
select() // pick columns
mutate() // add new computed column
arrange() // change order of rows in ascending and descending
group_by() + summarize() // groups rows by a common function using a specific operation
case_when() // regrouping row values

Census and ACS
The Decennial Census surveys essentially the entire population in 10 years. Census geography goes in the following order:
STATE
COUNTY
TRACT (“Neighborhood” around 5,000-8,000, changing boundaries)
BLOCK GROUP (higher MOE, Decennial Census only)

The American Community Survey (ACS) became a thing in around 2005, surveying about 3% of households to provide an estimate for the larger population. The ACS previously had a survey that was conducted every 3 years, however, that no longer exists. The 1-year ACS data exists for geographic areas with more than 65,000 people. The 5-year ACS data exists at the block group and tract level. ACS data includes an estimate and a margin of error (MOE)
GEOIDs
GEOIDs are a unique gegraphic identifier code. The first two digits indicate the state, the following three indicate the county, and the last 5-6 indicate the tract.
‘tidycensus’ Functions

load_variables() // provides a codebook of variable names
get_acs() // retrieves data from Census API  

Example: data <- get_acs(geography = “county”,
variables = c(“B19013_001”, “B01003_001”),
state = “PA”,
year = 2023,
survey = “acs5”)

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be. Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I am looking at the estimated number of individuals with bachelors degrees in all 14 counties across Massachusetts. Here, I will look at how counties of varying population sizes produce more or less reliable estimates of population characteristics, specifically the number of individuals with bachelors degrees. This analysis will shed light on how the surveys that rely on random samples to generalize population characteristics, like the American Community Survey, may inaccurately represent areas with smaller populations.

section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

The area with the largest margin of error relative to its estimate is Dukes County, with a margin of error percent approximately 17.6%. Because Dukes County has a smaller estimate and higher margin of error, this makes the ACS estimate less reliable.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(bachelors = my_variable,
                pop = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                             bachelorsE bachelorsM   popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                                 <dbl>      <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 25001 Barnstable County, Massachusetts      46953       1690 230073    NA
2 25003 Berkshire County, Massachusetts       19480       1015 128047    NA
3 25005 Bristol County, Massachusetts         79826       2184 578436    NA
4 25007 Dukes County, Massachusetts            4170        732  20751    NA
5 25009 Essex County, Massachusetts          140926       2477 807258    NA
6 25011 Franklin County, Massachusetts        11576        629  70922    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = bachelorsM / bachelorsE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         10        675838.
2 Low confidence           1         20751 
3 Moderate                 3         71089.


The average population of high-confidence counties in Massachusetts is 675,837. The average population of low-confidence counties in Massachusetts is 20,751; however, it is worth nothing that only one county is considered in this average. This suggests that counties with higher populations have lower margins of error, producing more reliable estimates. At the county-level, due to the larger size of most counties, this is not a glaring issue in many cases. However, when working with more granular geographies (i.e., tract-level, block group-level), this effect can produce misleading estimates.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
Based on the analysis, the two counties we know the least about are Dukes County and Nantucket County. Interestingly enough, both counties are small island counties with active county governments, home to Nantucket and Martha’s Vineyard.
The American Community Survey (ACS) works by targeting 3.5 million addresses annually as opposed to collecting data from all households in decade intervals like the Census. Because of this, the ACS relies on these samples to produce representative estimates at each geographic level, excluding block groups. The ACS has two survey versions: a one-year survey, which provides estimates for areas with at least 65,000 people, and a five-year survey, which provides estimates of all population-level areas. Because the ACS relies on a random sample of addresses to accurately estimate data points, smaller geographic areas receive less representation, making them more likely to have less representative estimates.
If a state agency were to view data across differently populated areas the same, this would result in less-populated, likely rural areas from receiving fair representation in receiving state resources. For example, if an agency were to rely on ACS estimates to fairly allocate housing funds to Scranton, with a population of around 75,000 people, vs. Wellsboro, with a population of 3,472 people, an area like Wellsboro would like receive more variable/inconsistent funding compared to an area like Scranton with a larger population.

text:
Changing the geographic scale

county_wide_tract <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = c(bachelors = my_variable,
                pop = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  county = "Barnstable",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

# compute the margin of error percent for bachelors degrees in Barnstable #

barnstable_moe <- county_wide_tract %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = bachelorsM / bachelorsE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 20  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 30 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(barnstable_moe, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence     7
2 Low confidence     15
3 Moderate           35

head(barnstable_moe)

# A tibble: 6 × 8
  GEOID       NAME         bachelorsE bachelorsM  popE  popM moe_pct reliability
  <chr>       <chr>             <dbl>      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl> <chr>      
1 25001010100 Census Trac…        965        227  3681    23    23.5 Moderate   
2 25001010206 Census Trac…        790        184  4371   288    23.3 Moderate   
3 25001010208 Census Trac…        228        111  1675   287    48.7 Low confid…
4 25001010304 Census Trac…        629        172  2745   314    27.3 Moderate   
5 25001010306 Census Trac…        616        185  3027   316    30.0 Low confid…
6 25001010400 Census Trac…        815        219  3335   419    26.9 Moderate   

# compare different levels or reliability in Barnstable #

barnstable_moe %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_tracts = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_tracts avg_population
  <chr>              <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence        7          4326.
2 Low confidence        15          3731.
3 Moderate              35          4109.


In the code above, I chose to calculate the estimated count of individuals in Barnstable, MA that have a bachelors degree at the tract-level. To calculate the confidence levels, I adjusted the threshold for what is considered high confidence to be slightly more flexible, since tracts are a smaller geographic area than counties and inherently require a bit more flexibility.Thus, tracts with high confidence level have a margin of error percent less than 20%, tracts with a moderate confidence level have a margin of error percent between 20% and 30%, and tracts with a low confidence level have a margin of error percent greater then 30%. After grouping tracts by confidence levels and calculating the average population in each, it is clear that the pattern from the previous exercise holds. Tracts with higher confidence levels have an average population of 4,326 per tract, whereas areas with low confidence levels have an average population of 3,730.
This supplemental analysis provides evidence that discrepancies in population even at a smaller scale can yield even bigger disparities in estimates. While at the county-level a 100 or 1,000 person difference in population may not yield vastly different confidence levels, at the tract-level, this can result in glaring disparities in confidence level estimates.

title: Week 3: ggplot and data viz
text:
Key Concepts
Different types of ggplots
If I want to know how a variable is spread… use geom_histogram()

If I want to know how two variables relate… use geom_point()

If I want to see how two groups compare… use geom_boxplot() or geom_col()

If I want to see how things change over time… use geom_line()

If I want to see how uncertain a value is… use geom_errorbar()

If I want to see multiple plots for different categories… use facet_wrap(~variable)

Statistics terms
Coefficient of Variation (CV) is the relative measure of sampling error. The standard error tells us how confident we can be that an estimate is reflective of the true population. For the Census Bureau, a low confidence interval is around 15% (high reliability), medium confidence interval is around 15%-30%, and a high confidence interval is 30% or above (high sampling error).
Derived Uncertainty - moe_sum() // adding estimates together - moe_prop() // one estimate as a share of another - moe_ratio() // one not a subset of another
The standard error of difference is sqrt(se1^2 + se2^2).

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text:
Getting started
Here, I am going to explore the claims that were made by this article stating that white poverty has exploded and that poverty rates have disproportionately spiked in certain neighborhoods in Philadelphia between 2010 and 2017. The article relies on data from the 2006-2010 and the 2013-2017 5-Year American Community Survey’s (ACS) to draw these conclusions. To investigate this claim, I will look at estimated impoverished individuals, impoverished white individuals, white population, total population, and median income to establish whether or not these claims are overstated or statistically sound.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text:
Establishing neighborhoods
Specifically, the article makes the argument that the Eastwick neighborhood in Philadelphia has experienced the highest increase in poverty rate compared to the rest of the city between 2010 and 2017. The article also makes the argument that the Holmesburg neighborhood has experienced a large increase in white poverty rates, jumping from 2% to 19%. The last claim is that the Tioga neighborhood experienced the largest drop in median income in the city. The article does not specifically outline which Census tracts make up individual neighborhoods, so I am going to rely on the OpenDataPhilly Neighborhood designation to best approximate comparisons between neighborhoods. For areas with no recorded population (8 Census tracts), I will remove them from the data.


Show code
## Load neighborhoods shapefile ##
neighborhoods <- read_sf("data/philadelphia-neighborhoods")

# Join neighborhoods and census-tract data, assigning a tract to the neighborhood it shares the most overlap with #

# Ensure same coordinate system and transform if needed #

check_crs <- st_crs(neighborhoods)==st_crs(data2017)

neighborhoods <- st_transform(neighborhoods, st_crs(data2017))

neighborhoods <- st_make_valid(neighborhoods)

# Find the intersection between neighborhood and tract data #

neighborhoods_tracts2017 <- st_intersection(data2017, neighborhoods)

neighborhoods_tracts2010 <- st_intersection(data2010, neighborhoods)

# Assign tract to neighborhood they share most overlap with #

neighborhoods_tracts2017$area_overlap <- st_area(neighborhoods_tracts2017)

neighborhoods_tracts2010$area_overlap <- st_area(neighborhoods_tracts2010)

data2017 <- neighborhoods_tracts2017 %>%
  group_by(GEOID) %>%
  slice_max(area_overlap)

data2010 <- neighborhoods_tracts2010 %>%
  group_by(GEOID) %>%
  slice_max(area_overlap)

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text:
City-level analysis
First, I will look at how the citywide poverty rate, white poverty rate, and median income has changed between 2010 and 2017.

              rename(nhood_name=NAME.1) %>%
              # there is no reported MOE for total population #
              mutate(poverty_prop = povertyE/total_popE,

Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
Build a half-mile zone around every station and merge the circles into one shape. Remember your units.

station_zone <- stations %>%
  st_buffer(dist = 5280/2) %>%
  st_union()

Pick whole cookies: which tracts don’t touch the zone at all?

outside_zone <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_filter(station_zone, .predicate = st_intersects)

nrow(outside_zone)

[1] 229


Cut the dough: what share of each tract’s area falls inside the zone?

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(tract_area = as.numeric(st_area(.)))

covered <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_intersection(station_zone) %>%
  mutate(covered_area = as.numeric(st_area(.))) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(GEOID, covered_area)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  left_join(covered, by = "GEOID") %>%
  mutate(pct_covered = replace_na(covered_area / tract_area, 0) * 100)

Notice: that last step is the left_join() from Part 1b. It’s a join by what (GEOID), used to bring a join-by-where result back into the table. The two kinds of join work together.

title: Week 4: GIS in R
text:
Key Concepts
Review - The Census operates based on a 90% confidence interval to calculate the MOE - You then take the MOE and divide it by 1,645 to get the standard error. Then, you do the standard error difference which is sqrt(se1^2 + se2^2)
Spatial Data Function - get_acs(…, geometry = TRUE) // creates the tidycensus data as a shapefile (sf) - st_set_crs() // adding the correct label - st_transform(data, coordinate type) // change the coordinate system - st_crs() // gets the coordinate system of the data - st_buffer(data, units of the layer) // create a buffer zone around a data point - st_intersects() // data points share a border with each other or are situated within each other - st_touches() // only if two polygons or lines touch each other - st_within() // only if one polygon is located within another - st_filer() // count the tract - st_intersection() // shapes change and more shape - st_union // append? - st_join // works like a normal join, just spatially - st_distance // returns a matrix with the distance between all of your stations and tracts
Coordinate Reference Systems (CRS) Geographic coordinates live on a sphere, and are measured in the degrees as angular measurements form the center of the Earth.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text:
Analyzing poverty
First, I will look at how the citywide poverty rate has changed between 2010 and 2017 in each Census tract.
There are 81 neighborhoods in Philadelphia that display having statistically distinguishable change in poverty rates from zero at a 90% confidence interval, whereas the remaining 81 neighborhoods did not display a statistically distinguishable change in poverty rates. This means that any observed change in poverty rates in those 81 neighborhoods could be due to sampling noise at a 90% confidence interval.


Show code
#| code-fold: true

## Remove tracts with 0 population ##

data2010 <- data2010 %>%
            filter(total_popE > 0)

data2017 <- data2017 %>%
            filter(total_popE > 0)

## Check for NAs in the data ##

#sum(is.na(data2010$povertyE))
#sum(is.na(data2010$total_popE))

## Compute poverty rate across neighborhoods ##

data2010_poverty <- data2010 %>%
              rename("nhood_name"="NAME.1") %>%
              group_by(nhood_name) %>%
              # there is no reported MOE for total population so I assume it is 0 #
              summarise(neighborhood_total_poverty2010 = sum(povertyE),
                    neighborhood_total_pop2010 = sum(total_popE),
                    neighborhood_total_moe2010 = moe_sum(povertyM, povertyE)) %>%
              mutate(neighborhood_povertyshare2010 = neighborhood_total_poverty2010/neighborhood_total_pop2010,
                    neighborhood_povertyshare_moe2010 = moe_prop(neighborhood_total_poverty2010, neighborhood_total_pop2010, neighborhood_total_moe2010, 0))

data2017_poverty <- data2017 %>%
              rename("nhood_name"="NAME.1") %>%
              group_by(nhood_name) %>%
              # there is no reported MOE for total population so I assume it is 0 #
              summarise(neighborhood_total_poverty2017 = sum(povertyE),
                    neighborhood_total_pop2017 = sum(total_popE),
                    neighborhood_total_moe2017 = moe_sum(povertyM, povertyE)) %>%
              mutate(neighborhood_povertyshare2017 = neighborhood_total_poverty2017/neighborhood_total_pop2017,
                    neighborhood_povertyshare_moe2017 = moe_prop(neighborhood_total_poverty2017, neighborhood_total_pop2017, neighborhood_total_moe2017, 0))

## Join data 

compareyrs_poverty <- data2017_poverty %>%
              st_drop_geometry %>%
              left_join(data2010_poverty, by="nhood_name") %>%
              mutate(
              change = neighborhood_povertyshare2017 - neighborhood_povertyshare2010,
              se_1     = neighborhood_povertyshare_moe2010 / 1.645,
              se_2     = neighborhood_povertyshare_moe2017 / 1.645,
              se_diff  = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
              moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
              z        = change / se_diff,
              significant = abs(z) > 1.645
  )

true_sig_poverty <- compareyrs_poverty %>%
  count(significant)

## Check Eastwick ##

eastwick <- compareyrs_poverty %>%
  arrange(desc(change))




Show code
## Create error bar plot ##

compareyrs_poverty %>%
  filter(significant) %>% 
  mutate(nhood_name = str_replace(nhood_name, "_", " ")) %>%
  arrange(desc(change)) %>%
  head(10) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(nhood_name, change), y = change)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = "Estimated change")) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = change - moe_diff,
                    ymax = change + moe_diff), width = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Statistically significant change in poverty rate",
       subtitle = "2006–2010 vs 2013–20217, ACS 5-year estimates",
       x = NULL, y = "Philadelphia Neighborhood",
       fill = NULL)









In exploring the claim that Eastwick has showed the greatest poverty rate increase of any community, it appears that other neighborhoods have emerged as experiencing greater rates of poverty. Namely, neighborhoods like Caroll Park, Packer Park, East Kensington, Aston Woodbridge, and Pennrose experience the sharpest increases in poverty at a rate statistically distinguishable from zero.

text:
Main Takeaways
After investigating the claims made by the WHYY article, it is clear that interpretation of ACS data is not straightforwarf, especially when comparing data between different time periods. More granular geographic areas require attention as sampling small populations can leave room for noise in the data. In the case of this article, misinterpretation or failing to further investigate the change in the margin of error can lead to overstating claims. Again, it is important to consider that the original author may have used different neighborhood boundaries. Stil, the claim that Eastwick experienced the highest rate of poverty increase is largely unsupported by the data, whereas the claim that Holmesburg experienced a drastic - approximately 17% percentage point - increase in white poverty cannot be determined by current methods and available data. Furthermore, the claim that the Tioga neighborhood experienced the largest drop in median income is unsupported based on my analysis.

Analyzing poverty: Eastwick
First, I will look at how the poverty rate has changed between 2010 and 2017 in each neighborhood to determine if Eastwick experienced the highest increase in poverty rate.
There are 81 neighborhoods in Philadelphia that display having statistically distinguishable change in poverty rates from zero at a 90% confidence interval, whereas the remaining 58 neighborhoods did not display a statistically distinguishable change in poverty rates. This means that any observed change in poverty rates in those 58 neighborhoods could be due to sampling noise at a 90% confidence interval.

## Remove tracts with 0 population ##

data2010 <- data2010 %>%

              # there is no reported MOE for total population so I assume it is 0 #
              summarise(neighborhood_total_poverty2010 = sum(povertyE),
                    neighborhood_total_pop2010 = sum(total_popE),
                    neighborhood_total_moe2010 = moe_sum(povertyM, povertyE)) %>%
              mutate(neighborhood_povertyshare2010 = neighborhood_total_poverty2010/neighborhood_total_pop2010,
                    neighborhood_povertyshare_moe2010 = moe_prop(neighborhood_total_poverty2010, neighborhood_total_pop2010, neighborhood_total_moe2010, 0))

              mutate(neighborhood_povertyshare2017 = neighborhood_total_poverty2017/neighborhood_total_pop2017,

              st_drop_geometry %>%

              se_diff  = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),

Analyzing poverty: Eastwick
First, I will look at how the poverty rate has changed between 2010 and 2017 in each neighborhood to determine if Eastwick experienced the highest increase in poverty rate.
There are 81 neighborhoods in Philadelphia that display having statistically distinguishable change in poverty rates from zero at a 90% confidence interval, whereas the remaining 58 neighborhoods did not display a statistically distinguishable change in poverty rates. This means that any observed change in poverty rates in those 58 neighborhoods could be due to sampling noise at a 90% confidence interval.


Show code

            filter(total_popE > 0)

data2010_poverty <- data2010 %>%
              rename("nhood_name"="NAME.1") %>%
              group_by(nhood_name) %>%
              # there is no reported MOE for total population so I assume it is 0 #
              summarise(neighborhood_total_poverty2010 = sum(povertyE),
                    neighborhood_total_pop2010 = sum(total_popE),
                    neighborhood_total_moe2010 = moe_sum(povertyM, povertyE)) %>%
              mutate(neighborhood_povertyshare2010 = neighborhood_total_poverty2010/neighborhood_total_pop2010,
                    neighborhood_povertyshare_moe2010 = moe_prop(neighborhood_total_poverty2010, neighborhood_total_pop2010, neighborhood_total_moe2010, 0))

data2017_poverty <- data2017 %>%
              rename("nhood_name"="NAME.1") %>%
              group_by(nhood_name) %>%
              # there is no reported MOE for total population so I assume it is 0 #
              summarise(neighborhood_total_poverty2017 = sum(povertyE),
                    neighborhood_total_pop2017 = sum(total_popE),
                    neighborhood_total_moe2017 = moe_sum(povertyM, povertyE)) %>%
              mutate(neighborhood_povertyshare2017 = neighborhood_total_poverty2017/neighborhood_total_pop2017,
                    neighborhood_povertyshare_moe2017 = moe_prop(neighborhood_total_poverty2017, neighborhood_total_pop2017, neighborhood_total_moe2017, 0))

## Join data 

compareyrs_poverty <- data2017_poverty %>%
              st_drop_geometry %>%
              left_join(data2010_poverty, by="nhood_name") %>%
              mutate(
              change = neighborhood_povertyshare2017 - neighborhood_povertyshare2010,
              se_1     = neighborhood_povertyshare_moe2010 / 1.645,
              se_2     = neighborhood_povertyshare_moe2017 / 1.645,
              se_diff  = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
              moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
              z        = change / se_diff,

In exploring the claim that Eastwick has showed the greatest poverty rate increase of any community, it appears that other neighborhoods have emerged as experiencing greater rates of poverty. Thus, based upon my analysis, the article’s claim that Eastwick experienced the highest increase in poverty rate out of any Philadelphia neighborhood is unsupported.
